landmarks.name: Old Havana
landmarks.writeup: A UNESCO World Heritage site known for its well-preserved Spanish colonial architecture and vibrant street life.

wiki.extract: Old Havana is the city-center (downtown) and one of the 15 municipalities forming Havana, Cuba. It has the second highest population density in the city and contains the core of the original city of Havana. The positions of the original Walls of Havana are the modern boundaries of Old Havana.

landmarks.name: El Morro Castle
landmarks.writeup: A historic fortress guarding the entrance to Havana Bay, built in the 16th century.

wiki.extract:
The Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro, also known as Castillo del Morro, is a fortress guarding the entrance to the Havana harbor.
The design is by the Italian engineer Battista Antonelli (1547–1616). Originally under the control of Spain, the fortress was captured by the British in 1762 and returned to Spain under the Treaty of Paris (1763) a year later. The Morro Castle was the primary defence in the Havana harbor until La Cabaña was completed in 1774.

landmarks.name: Varadero Beach
landmarks.writeup: One of the largest resort areas in the Caribbean, famous for its white sandy beaches and clear waters.

wiki.extract: Varadero, also referred to as Playa Azul, is a resort town in the province of Matanzas, Cuba, and one of the largest resort areas in the Caribbean. Varadero Beach is rated one of the world's best beaches in TripAdvisor's Traveler's Choice Awards since 2019, ranking at number 9 as of January 2024. Common activities include fishing and excursions to Matanzas, Cárdenas, and the Península de Zapata.

landmarks.name: Trinidad
landmarks.writeup: A colonial town with cobblestone streets and colorful buildings, also a UNESCO World Heritage site.

wiki.extract: Trinidad is a town in the province of Sancti Spíritus, central Cuba. Together with the nearby Valle de los Ingenios, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988, because of its historical importance as a center of the sugar trade in the 18th and 19th centuries. Trinidad is one of the best-preserved cities in the Caribbean from the time when the sugar trade was the main industry in the region.

landmarks.name: Che Guevara Mausoleum
landmarks.writeup: The resting place of revolutionary leader Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, located in Santa Clara.

wiki.extract: The Che Guevara Mausoleum is a memorial in Santa Clara, Cuba, located in "Plaza Che Guevara". It houses the remains of the revolutionary Ernesto "Che" Guevara and 29 fellow combatants killed in 1967 during Guevara's attempt to spur an armed uprising in Bolivia. The full area, which contains a bronze 22-foot statue of Guevara, is referred to as the Ernesto Guevara Sculptural Complex.

cultural_events.name: Havana International Jazz Festival
cultural_events.writeup: An annual event attracting international jazz musicians and enthusiasts.

cultural_events.name: Carnival of Santiago de Cuba
cultural_events.writeup: A vibrant festival featuring music, dance, and colorful parades celebrating Afro-Cuban culture.

wiki.extract: Whether they are called carnavales, charangas or parrandas, large public celebrations dating at least as far back as the 17th century are common throughout Cuba. However, among Cubans, the Carnaval of Santiago de Cuba enjoys a special status.

cultural_events.name: Havana Biennial
cultural_events.writeup: A contemporary art exhibition showcasing Latin American and Caribbean artists.

wiki.extract: The Bienal de La Habana was a traditional Latin, Caribbean event, originated in Havana, Cuba, that aims to raise awareness to promote contemporary art and giving priority to Latin-American and Caribbean artists.

food_writeup: Cuban cuisine blends Spanish, African, and Caribbean influences, featuring dishes like ropa vieja (shredded beef), black beans and rice, and plantains.
brief_history: Cuba was colonized by Spain in the 15th century, gained independence in 1902, and underwent a communist revolution in 1959 led by Fidel Castro. It has since been a one-party socialist state.
current_conflicts: Cuba faces ongoing economic challenges and political tensions, including strained relations with the United States and internal calls for political reform.

commentary.inflation_management: Cuba has no conventional inflation-targeting regime; the central bank is subordinate to the state plan and monetary policy is conducted mainly through exchange and price controls. For decades the dual-currency system (CUC alongside the CUP) hid underlying pressures. The January 1, 2021 ordenamiento ended dual currency and devalued the official rate to 24 CUP per dollar, but persistent shortages, a large informal exchange market, and dollarization of basic goods have produced a sustained high-inflation environment since, far above anything in the pre-2021 controlled system. Without market-determined interest rates or an open capital account, the authorities have few standard tools to anchor expectations, and prices are effectively set by the availability of dollars in the informal market.
commentary.debt_management: Cuba's debt record cannot be quantified from the IMF dataset, since the country has no published series, but its broad shape is well documented: decades of external arrears, limited market access, and dependence on bilateral lenders. A 2015 Paris Club restructuring wrote down a large share of its Soviet-era debt arrears, offering some breathing room, but financing constraints tightened again as Venezuelan oil support faded and US sanctions intensified from 2017 onward. The COVID-era collapse of tourism and the 2021 monetary reform (ordenamiento) worsened the hard-currency position, and by the mid-2020s renewed power-blackout spending and import dependence had left the external accounts under severe strain. Debt management in Cuba is less a fiscal choice than a function of sanctions, ally support, and export earnings.

key_events.event: US-Cuba diplomatic normalization under the Obama administration eased remittance and travel flows.
Monetary ordenamiento ended the dual currency system and devalued the peso (Jan 1, 2021); July 2021 protests were the largest in decades amid shortages.
Severe fuel shortages and aging grid triggered nationwide blackouts, deepening the economic crisis.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Without IMF data, any quantitative outlook would be fabrication; the qualitative picture is one of a country in a prolonged structural crisis. The base case is stagnation with chronic shortages unless remittances, tourism, or external financing materially improve. Key uncertainties are US policy direction, the durability of allies' support, and whether the government loosens central control over markets. A gradual reform path could stabilize the decade, but the evidence of the last five years points more toward continued strain than turnaround.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. No IMF data series is available for Cuba, so all commentary here is qualitative and cannot quote IMF debt, inflation, or GDP figures.
